reviewer: Codex research agent, delegated researcher and verifier
scope: Eight individually researched candidates from Arlington's official notable-graves collections. No national-queue blanket approval, photos, or exact grave pins. Public-profile flags checked and no selected QID was marked already public. Day precision is withheld where only years have completed review. Independent editorial audit required before release.

candidates.name: Grace Hopper
candidates.short_description: Computer-science pioneer, mathematician, and U.S. Navy rear admiral.
candidates.biography: Grace Hopper combined a career in mathematics with decades of naval service. She programmed Harvard's Mark I and later worked on UNIVAC and programming-language development. Her work helped make computers more accessible to people writing software. She is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
candidates.why_interesting: Her career connected early room-sized computers with the development of modern programming languages.

burial_evidence.notes: Arlington lists Hopper's actual grave, Section 59, Grave 973. Naval History and Heritage Command confirms exact birth and January 1, 1992 death; the latter fills the collector's null date, not an inferred January 1 placeholder. Navy biography supports computer science, mathematics and naval service tags. Local QID, article, and lifetime align. No claim that she invented COBOL alone. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.

candidates.name: John Glenn
candidates.short_description: First American to orbit Earth, Marine pilot, and U.S. senator from Ohio.
candidates.biography: John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth in 1962 aboard Friendship 7. Before joining NASA, he flew as a Marine pilot in World War II and Korea. He later represented Ohio in the U.S. Senate and returned to space aboard Discovery in 1998 at age 77. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
candidates.why_interesting: Thirty-six years separated his first orbital flight from his return to space at age 77.

burial_evidence.notes: Arlington's astronauts page lists Section 35, Grave 1543, confirming actual interment. NASA gives exact birth/death dates and supports astronaut, Marine, and senator identity. Military, politics, and history tags reflect these roles; astronaut is not automatically classified as scientist. NASA and Arlington's astronauts page both place his shuttle return in 1998; the 1988 typo on Arlington's separate prominent-military page is rejected. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.

candidates.name: Joe Louis
candidates.short_description: World heavyweight boxing champion and World War II Army veteran.
candidates.biography: Joe Louis became world heavyweight boxing champion in 1937 after defeating James J. Braddock. His success made him a nationally celebrated athlete during a period of deep racial division. During World War II he served in the Army and boxed in exhibitions for troops. He was buried with military honors at Arlington National Cemetery.
candidates.why_interesting: His boxing career made him a national figure, and his Army service took his exhibition bouts to troops overseas.

burial_evidence.notes: Arlington's sports listing identifies the boxer and actual grave, Section 7A, Grave 177. NPS confirms championship, Army service and burial. Smithsonian's transcription of his interment program supplies exact dates and full identity Joe Louis (Barrow): https://nmaahc.si.edu/object/nmaahc_2013.46.25.5. Sports, military, and history tags reflect documented careers. Local QID/article match; no image of the program reused. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.

candidates.name: Thurgood Marshall
candidates.short_description: Civil-rights lawyer and the first Black justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.
candidates.biography: Thurgood Marshall fought racial segregation as a lawyer before becoming the first Black justice of the U.S. Supreme Court. His victories included Brown v. Board of Education, the decision rejecting racial segregation in public schools. He served on the Supreme Court from 1967 until his retirement in 1991. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
candidates.why_interesting: He helped reshape American law both as the lawyer arguing landmark cases and as a Supreme Court justice.

burial_evidence.notes: Arlington confirms the justice's actual grave, Section 5, Grave 40-3, plus civil-rights litigation and Brown v. Board role. Federal Judicial Center confirms exact July 2, 1908 birth and January 24, 1993 death and court service. A separate uscourts.gov educational page's June 2 birth is inconsistent with FJC and Arlington's civil-rights walking-tour record and is rejected. Civil-rights, government/politics, and history tags are supported; no unsupported judges slug. Local QID/article identify the justice. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.

candidates.name: Medgar Evers
candidates.short_description: Mississippi civil-rights organizer, NAACP field secretary, and World War II Army veteran.
candidates.biography: Medgar Evers organized voter-registration drives and challenged segregation as the NAACP's Mississippi field secretary. A World War II Army veteran, he helped build support for civil rights despite repeated threats. He was assassinated outside his Jackson home in June 1963 and was buried with military honors at Arlington National Cemetery.
candidates.why_interesting: His work connected local voter registration and economic boycotts with the national struggle against segregation.

burial_evidence.notes: Arlington confirms actual interment, Section 36, Grave 1431. VA History explicitly gives July 2, 1925 birth and June 12, 1963 death and supports Army and civil-rights roles. NPS's generic person page incorrectly says July 12 death; June 12 is independently supported by Arlington and the Evers Home National Monument's Long-Delayed Justice article. Civil-rights, military and history tags do not infer a crime career from being a murder victim. Local QID and article identity match. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.

candidates.name: Charles Young
candidates.short_description: Army officer and the first Black national park superintendent.
candidates.biography: Charles Young overcame racial barriers to graduate from West Point and build a career as an Army officer, teacher, and diplomat. In 1903 he became the first Black national park superintendent while leading troops at Sequoia National Park. After his death in Nigeria, his remains were returned to the United States and buried at Arlington National Cemetery in 1923.
candidates.why_interesting: His Army assignments included protecting Sequoia's landscape and improving its roads and trails.

burial_evidence.notes: NPS gives exact dates and describes initial Nigeria burial followed by June 1, 1923 Arlington reinterment, Section 3, Grave 1730-B. The current resting place is Arlington, not his death site. Identity collision resolved by Q5083782, the specific Army-officer Wikipedia article, lifetime, and NPS career account. Military, civil-rights and history tags follow NPS's explicit characterization; no hobby-based music tag. His general rank was posthumous in 2021, not a lifetime rank. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.

candidates.name: Lee Marvin
candidates.short_description: Academy Award-winning actor and World War II Marine veteran.
candidates.biography: Lee Marvin brought a commanding presence to Westerns and action films, including The Dirty Dozen and The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. His performance in Cat Ballou earned an Academy Award. Before his acting career, he served in the Marines during World War II and was wounded at Saipan. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
candidates.why_interesting: The actor behind memorable screen tough guys had served in the Pacific before his Hollywood career.

burial_evidence.notes: Arlington identifies actor Lee Marvin and actual grave, Section 7A, Grave 176; its film and military account supports the biography and entertainment/military/history tags. VA independently supports identity and service. Independent audit agent verified exact dates on page 18 of Arlington's school walking tour: https://education.arlingtoncemetery.mil/Portals/2/WWII%20Walking%20Tour-School%20Tour.pdf. Local QID and Lee_Marvin article distinguish him from military namesakes. No combat anecdote beyond documented Saipan wounding. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.

candidates.name: Walter Reed
candidates.short_description: Army physician and researcher whose team confirmed mosquito transmission of yellow fever.
candidates.biography: Walter Reed was an Army physician and medical researcher whose team helped establish that mosquitoes transmit yellow fever. He also served as curator of the Army Medical Museum and taught at the Army Medical School. His name became associated with one of the country's best-known military medical centers. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
candidates.why_interesting: The familiar hospital name belongs to a researcher whose work changed the understanding of yellow fever.

burial_evidence.notes: Arlington lists physician Walter Reed's actual grave, Section 3, Grave 1864, and yellow-fever research. National Museum of Health and Medicine confirms September 13, 1851 birth, death year 1902, Army service, and museum/teaching work. Exact death date is withheld: independent audit found November 23 in Arlington's medicine walking tour versus November 22 in NCPC's 2017 plaque report. The museum article's inconsistent age-at-death statement is not repeated. Scientists, military and history tags reflect research and Army roles. Q613136 and Walter_Reed article identify the physician, not his son Walter L. Reed. Coordinates are a cemetery reference point, not surveyed grave or entrance coordinates.
